snav-01-c1.text: Max-Planck-Gesellschaft (2009). Walking in circles. Max Planck Society research news.
snav-01-c1.quote: the belief that people walk in circles when lost is mainly based on anecdotal evidence and has never been studied systematically in a real desert or forest.
snav-01-c1.claim: until 2009 the belief rested mainly on anecdote

snav-01-c1.text: Max-Planck-Gesellschaft (2009). Walking in circles. Max Planck Society research news.
snav-01-c1.quote: examined the walking trajectories of people who walked for several hours in the Sahara desert (Tunisia) and in the Bienwald forest area (Germany)
snav-01-c1.claim: They tracked people with GPS as they tried to walk straight for several hours in the Sahara in Tunisia and in the Bienwald forest in Germany.

snav-01-c1.text: Max-Planck-Gesellschaft (2009). Walking in circles. Max Planck Society research news.
snav-01-c1.quote: The results showed that participants were only able to keep a straight path when the sun or moon was visible.
snav-01-c1.claim: The walkers kept a straight path only when the sun or moon was visible.

snav-01-c1.text: Max-Planck-Gesellschaft (2009). Walking in circles. Max Planck Society research news.
snav-01-c1.quote: However, as soon as the sun disappeared behind some clouds, people started to walk in circles without even noticing it.
snav-01-c1.claim: they started to walk in circles without even noticing

snav-01-c1.text: Max-Planck-Gesellschaft (2009). Walking in circles. Max Planck Society research news.
snav-01-c1.quote: Most of the participants in the study walked in circles, sometimes in extremely small ones (diameter less than 20 metres).
snav-01-c1.claim: Blindfolded, most volunteers walked in circles, some less than 20 metres across.

snav-01-c1.text: Max-Planck-Gesellschaft (2009). Walking in circles. Max Planck Society research news.
snav-01-c1.quote: Instead, the same person sometimes veered to the left, sometimes to the right.
snav-01-c1.claim: the same person veered left one time and right the next

snav-01-c1.text: Max-Planck-Gesellschaft (2009). Walking in circles. Max Planck Society research news.
snav-01-c1.quote: Small random errors in the various sensory signals that provide information about walking direction add up over time
snav-01-c1.claim: Small random errors in the senses that tell you which way you are walking add up over time

snav-01-c1.text: Max-Planck-Gesellschaft (2009). Walking in circles. Max Planck Society research news.
snav-01-c1.quote: People need to use reliable cues for walking direction in their environment, for example a tower or mountain in the distance, or the position of the sun.
snav-01-c1.claim: a tower or mountain in the distance, or the sun

snav-01-c1.text: Ole Edward Wattne, Frode Volden (2023). Waylosing and wayfinding in the outdoors: a typology of wayfinding approaches to problem-solving when temporarily lost. The Journal of Navigation.
snav-01-c1.quote: the lost person is unable to identify or orient his present location with respect to known locations
snav-01-c1.claim: unable to identify or orient their present location with respect to known locations

snav-01-c1.text: Ole Edward Wattne, Frode Volden (2023). Waylosing and wayfinding in the outdoors: a typology of wayfinding approaches to problem-solving when temporarily lost. The Journal of Navigation.
snav-01-c1.quote: This information comes from structured interviews with rescued lost persons, conducted soon after (sometimes during) their recovery, and tested through survey research and interviews with 120 deer hunters in Nova Scotia
snav-01-c1.claim: surveyed 120 deer hunters in Nova Scotia

snav-01-c1.text: Ole Edward Wattne, Frode Volden (2023). Waylosing and wayfinding in the outdoors: a typology of wayfinding approaches to problem-solving when temporarily lost. The Journal of Navigation.
Ole Edward Wattne, Frode Volden (2023). Waylosing and wayfinding in the outdoors: a typology of wayfinding approaches to problem-solving when temporarily lost. The Journal of Navigation.
snav-01-c1.quote: With the majority of data collected from the United Sates (91%), followed by New Zealand (5%), Canada (2%)
snav-01-c1.claim: 91% of them came from the United States

snav-01-c2.text: US Forest Service. If You Get Lost. USDA Forest Service.
snav-01-c2.quote: As soon as you realize you may be lost: stop, stay calm, stay put. Panic is your greatest enemy.
snav-01-c2.claim: Stop, stay calm, stay put; panic is your greatest enemy.

snav-01-c2.text: US Forest Service. If You Get Lost. USDA Forest Service.
snav-01-c2.quote: Do not move at all until you have a specific reason to take a step.
snav-01-c2.claim: Do not move at all until you have a specific reason to take a step.

snav-01-c2.text: US Forest Service. If You Get Lost. USDA Forest Service.
snav-01-c2.quote: As a very last resort, follow a drainage or stream downhill.
snav-01-c2.claim: Following a drainage or stream downhill is a very last resort.

snav-01-c2.text: US Forest Service. If You Get Lost. USDA Forest Service.
snav-01-c2.quote: If you are not very, very confident in the route, then it’s always better to stay put.
snav-01-c2.claim: If you are not very, very confident of the route, stay put.

snav-01-c2.text: US Forest Service. If You Get Lost. USDA Forest Service.
snav-01-c2.quote: If it’s nightfall, you are injured or you are near exhaustion, stay in place.
snav-01-c2.claim: If night is falling, you are injured or you are near exhaustion, stay where you are.

snav-01-c2.text: San Diego Mountain Rescue Team. Hug-a-Tree and Survive. San Diego Mountain Rescue Team.
snav-01-c2.quote: Find a landmark — an actual tree, a large rock, any fixed point — and stay with it.
snav-01-c2.claim: Pick an actual tree, a large rock or any fixed point and stay with it.

snav-01-c2.text: San Diego Mountain Rescue Team. Hug-a-Tree and Survive. San Diego Mountain Rescue Team.
snav-01-c2.quote: Make noise — a whistle is best.

snav-01-c2.text: San Diego Mountain Rescue Team. Hug-a-Tree and Survive. San Diego Mountain Rescue Team.
snav-01-c2.quote: Leave footprints and clues where searchers can see them.
snav-01-c2.claim: leave clues where searchers can see them

snav-01-c2.text: US Forest Service. If You Get Lost. USDA Forest Service.
snav-01-c2.quote: Give them exact details of where you are going, the trail you plan to follow, when you will return, the vehicle you are driving (and where you plan to park)
snav-01-c2.claim: tell someone exactly where you are going, your route, when you will be back, what you are driving and where you will park

snav-01-c2.text: Mountain Rescue England and Wales. Safety. Mountain Rescue England and Wales.
snav-01-c2.quote: Dial 999 or 112. Ask for ‘Police’ then ‘Mountain Rescue’
snav-01-c2.claim: dial 999 or 112 and ask for Police, then Mountain Rescue

snav-01-c2.text: Mountain Rescue England and Wales. Safety. Mountain Rescue England and Wales.
snav-01-c2.quote: Do NOT change your position until contacted by the rescue team.
snav-01-c2.claim: do not change your position until the rescue team contacts you

snav-01-c2.text: RNZ Sunday Morning (2024). Search and rescue: the science of how lost people behave in the wild. RNZ.
snav-01-c2.quote: because if no search gets started for you, that's going to be a problem too.
snav-01-c2.claim: if no search gets started for you, that is a problem too

snav-01-c3.text: Amanda Hashimoto, Larkin Heintzman, Robert Koester, Nicole Abaid (2022). An agent-based model reveals lost person behavior based on data from wilderness search and rescue. Scientific Reports.
snav-01-c3.quote: The best fit profile contains over 50 % direction traveling, which is the behavior that causes the agent to travel the furthest among the rest.
snav-01-c3.claim: the best-fitting hiker spent over half its time travelling in one direction, the behaviour that carries a lost person furthest

snav-01-c3.text: Amanda Hashimoto, Larkin Heintzman, Robert Koester, Nicole Abaid (2022). An agent-based model reveals lost person behavior based on data from wilderness search and rescue. Scientific Reports.
snav-01-c3.quote: As time progresses, the survivability of the lost person decreases rapidly, especially so if the LP is not found within the first 51 hours
snav-01-c3.claim: Survival chances fall fast, especially if you are not found within the first 51 hours.

snav-01-c3.text: RNZ Sunday Morning (2024). Search and rescue: the science of how lost people behave in the wild. RNZ.
snav-01-c3.quote: If you get lost yourself, his best advice is to stay put.
snav-01-c3.claim: Robert Koester's best advice is to stay put

snav-01-c3.text: RNZ Sunday Morning (2024). Search and rescue: the science of how lost people behave in the wild. RNZ.
snav-01-c3.quote: You'll conserve your energy, you won't do anything stupid, you won't make the situation worse. It'll give you time to make a shelter, hopefully make a fire
snav-01-c3.claim: you conserve energy, you do not do anything stupid and you have time to make a shelter and a fire

snav-01-c3.text: Max-Planck-Gesellschaft (2009). Walking in circles. Max Planck Society research news.
snav-01-c3.quote: Instead, the same person sometimes veered to the left, sometimes to the right.
snav-01-c3.claim: the same walker curved left one time and right the next

snav-01-c3.text: San Diego Mountain Rescue Team. Navigation Basics. San Diego Mountain Rescue Team.
snav-01-c3.quote: Do not try to make the terrain fit your idea of where you are
snav-01-c3.claim: the trap of bending the map to fit

snav-01-c3.text: San Diego Mountain Rescue Team. Navigation Basics. San Diego Mountain Rescue Team.
snav-01-c3.quote: The ground is right. Stop, and back up to the last point where you were certain.
snav-01-c3.claim: the ground is right, so stop and back up to the last point where you were certain

snav-01-c3.text: RNZ Sunday Morning (2024). Search and rescue: the science of how lost people behave in the wild. RNZ.
snav-01-c3.quote: who usually kept going when they mistakenly think they're still on a trail
snav-01-c3.claim: lost hikers usually keep going when they wrongly think they are still on a trail

snav-01-c3.text: RNZ Sunday Morning (2024). Search and rescue: the science of how lost people behave in the wild. RNZ.
snav-01-c3.quote: When they're lost, they're more likely to go uphill, in pursuit of a cell phone signal.
snav-01-c3.claim: nowadays they often climb in search of a phone signal

snav-01-c3.text: San Diego Mountain Rescue Team. Hug-a-Tree and Survive. San Diego Mountain Rescue Team.
snav-01-c3.quote: In 1981, nine-year-old Jimmy Beveridge became separated from his family on Palomar Mountain, northeast of San Diego.
snav-01-c3.claim: In 1981 nine-year-old Jimmy Beveridge was separated from his family on Palomar Mountain, north-east of San Diego.

snav-01-c3.text: San Diego Mountain Rescue Team. Hug-a-Tree and Survive. San Diego Mountain Rescue Team.
snav-01-c3.quote: He was found four days later, dead of hypothermia, near a tree.
snav-01-c3.claim: He was found four days later, dead of hypothermia.

snav-01-c3.text: San Diego Mountain Rescue Team. Hug-a-Tree and Survive. San Diego Mountain Rescue Team.
snav-01-c3.quote: Border Patrol tracker Ab Taylor and others built Hug-a-Tree and Survive in response, so that no other family would go through it.
snav-01-c3.claim: A Border Patrol tracker, Ab Taylor, helped build a programme teaching children to stay with one tree

snav-01-c3.text: San Diego Mountain Rescue Team. Hug-a-Tree and Survive. San Diego Mountain Rescue Team.
snav-01-c3.quote: Hypothermia, not hunger or thirst, is what kills lost children.
snav-01-c3.claim: hypothermia, not hunger or thirst, is what kills lost children

snav-02-c1.text: Headquarters, Department of the Army (2002). FM 3-05.70: Survival. LSU Law Center (copy of the US Army field manual).
snav-02-c1.quote: In the Northern Hemisphere, they will move from west to east, and will point north at noon.
snav-02-c1.claim: in the Northern Hemisphere they swing from west to east and point north at noon

snav-02-c1.text: Astronomical Society of India, Public Outreach and Education Committee (2022). What do shadows tell you? Equinox. Astronomical Society of India.
Astronomical Society of India, Public Outreach and Education Committee (2022). What do shadows tell you? Equinox. Astronomical Society of India.
snav-02-c1.quote: On the equinox, the sun rises exactly East and sets exactly West.
snav-02-c1.claim: the sun rises exactly in the east and sets exactly in the west

snav-02-c1.text: Bruce McClure (2025). Look for equinox shadows in a direct line from west to east. EarthSky.
snav-02-c1.quote: the tip of a shadow traces a straight west-to-east path only at the equinoxes – applies everywhere worldwide, except at the North and South Poles
snav-02-c1.claim: the shadow tip of an upright stick follows a straight path from west to east all day, everywhere except the poles

snav-02-c1.text: Bruce McClure (2025). Look for equinox shadows in a direct line from west to east. EarthSky.
snav-02-c1.quote: Sundials are the earliest type of timekeeping device.
snav-02-c1.claim: the sundial is the earliest type of timekeeping device

snav-02-c1.text: Max-Planck-Gesellschaft (2009). Walking in circles. Max Planck Society research news.
snav-02-c1.quote: The results showed that participants were only able to keep a straight path when the sun or moon was visible.
snav-02-c1.claim: walkers held a course while they could see the sun or moon and lost it under cloud

snav-02-c1.text: Nainoa Thompson. Finding a Way: 1974-1980. Polynesian Voyaging Society archive.
snav-02-c1.quote: We use the sun when it is low down on the horizon.
snav-02-c1.claim: Nainoa Thompson uses the sun when it is low on the horizon

snav-02-c1.text: Nainoa Thompson. Finding a Way: 1974-1980. Polynesian Voyaging Society archive.
snav-02-c1.quote: When the sun gets too high, you steer by the waves.
snav-02-c1.claim: when the sun gets too high, he steers by the waves

snav-02-c2.text: Headquarters, Department of the Army (2002). FM 3-05.70: Survival. LSU Law Center (copy of the US Army field manual).
snav-02-c2.quote: This method is simple and accurate and consists of four steps
snav-02-c2.claim: The US Army's survival manual calls the shadow-tip method simple and accurate.

snav-02-c2.text: Headquarters, Department of the Army (2002). FM 3-05.70: Survival. LSU Law Center (copy of the US Army field manual).
snav-02-c2.quote: find a straight stick 1 meter (3 feet) long, and a level spot free of brush on which the stick will cast a definite shadow
snav-02-c2.claim: a straight stick about a metre long and a level spot, free of brush, where it casts a definite shadow

snav-02-c2.text: Headquarters, Department of the Army (2002). FM 3-05.70: Survival. LSU Law Center (copy of the US Army field manual).
snav-02-c2.quote: This first shadow mark is always west—everywhere on earth.
snav-02-c2.claim: This first mark is always west, everywhere on Earth.

snav-02-c2.text: Headquarters, Department of the Army (2002). FM 3-05.70: Survival. LSU Law Center (copy of the US Army field manual).
snav-02-c2.quote: Wait 10 to 15 minutes until the shadow tip moves a few centimeters.
snav-02-c2.claim: The tip moves a few centimetres.

snav-02-c2.text: Headquarters, Department of the Army (2002). FM 3-05.70: Survival. LSU Law Center (copy of the US Army field manual).
snav-02-c2.quote: Stand with the first mark (west) to your left and the second mark to your right—you are now facing north.
snav-02-c2.claim: Stand with the first mark on your left and the second on your right, and you are facing north

snav-02-c2.text: Headquarters, Department of the Army (2002). FM 3-05.70: Survival. LSU Law Center (copy of the US Army field manual).
snav-02-c2.quote: Draw a line through the two marks to get an accurate east-west line
snav-02-c2.claim: The line between the two marks is an accurate east-west line.

snav-02-c2.text: Headquarters, Department of the Army (2002). FM 3-05.70: Survival. LSU Law Center (copy of the US Army field manual).
snav-02-c2.quote: Bisect the angle between the hour hand and the 12-o’clock mark to get the north-south line
snav-02-c2.claim: halfway between the hour hand and 12 lies the north-south line

snav-02-c2.text: Headquarters, Department of the Army (2002). FM 3-05.70: Survival. LSU Law Center (copy of the US Army field manual).
snav-02-c2.quote: If your watch is set on daylight savings time, use the midway point between the hour hand and 1 o’clock to determine the north-south line.
snav-02-c2.claim: If the watch is on summer time, use 1 instead of 12.

snav-02-c2.text: Headquarters, Department of the Army (2002). FM 3-05.70: Survival. LSU Law Center (copy of the US Army field manual).
snav-02-c2.quote: In the Southern Hemisphere, point the watch’s 12-o’clock mark toward the sun; a midpoint halfway between 12 and the hour hand will give you the north-south line
snav-02-c2.claim: South of the equator, point 12 at the sun and take the midpoint between 12 and the hour hand.

snav-02-c2.text: Headquarters, Department of the Army (2002). FM 3-05.70: Survival. LSU Law Center (copy of the US Army field manual).
snav-02-c2.quote: If you only have a digital watch, draw a clock face on a circle of paper with the correct time on it and use it to determine your direction at that time.
snav-02-c2.claim: With only a digital watch, draw a clock face on paper showing the correct time and use that.

snav-02-c3.text: Astronomical Society of India, Public Outreach and Education Committee (2022). What do shadows tell you? Equinox. Astronomical Society of India.
snav-02-c3.quote: On the equinox, the sun rises exactly East and sets exactly West.
snav-02-c3.claim: It rises exactly east only around the equinoxes.

snav-02-c3.text: David P. Stern (2005). Sun Dial. NASA Goddard Space Flight Center, Sun-Earth Day.
snav-02-c3.quote: The location on the horizon of sunset (and sunrise) changes fastest at equinox.
snav-02-c3.claim: changing fastest at the equinoxes themselves

snav-02-c3.text: Headquarters, Department of the Army (2002). FM 3-05.70: Survival. LSU Law Center (copy of the US Army field manual).
snav-02-c3.quote: The direction will be accurate if you are using true local time, without any changes for daylight savings time.
snav-02-c3.claim: accurate only without any changes for daylight saving

snav-02-c3.text: Headquarters, Department of the Army (2002). FM 3-05.70: Survival. LSU Law Center (copy of the US Army field manual).
snav-02-c3.quote: Remember, the further you are from the equator, the more accurate this method will be.
snav-02-c3.claim: the further you are from the equator, the more accurate it is

snav-02-c3.text: Society for Popular Astronomy. Getting your bearings. Young Stargazers (Society for Popular Astronomy).
snav-02-c3.quote: The main one is that in summer, when British Summer Time is in force, midday (by the Sun) happens at 1 pm.
snav-02-c3.claim: during British Summer Time the sun's midday comes at 1 pm

snav-02-c3.text: Society for Popular Astronomy. Getting your bearings. Young Stargazers (Society for Popular Astronomy).
snav-02-c3.quote: variations in the Earth’s movement around the Sun mean that sometimes it is a little ahead of clock time, and sometimes behind
snav-02-c3.claim: puts it a little ahead of clock time or a little behind

snav-02-c3.text: Headquarters, Department of the Army (2002). FM 3-05.70: Survival. LSU Law Center (copy of the US Army field manual).
snav-02-c3.quote: This first shadow mark is always west—everywhere on earth.
snav-02-c3.claim: The first shadow mark is west everywhere on Earth

snav-02-c3.text: Headquarters, Department of the Army (2002). FM 3-05.70: Survival. LSU Law Center (copy of the US Army field manual).
snav-02-c3.quote: In the Southern Hemisphere, shadows will indicate south at noon.
snav-02-c3.claim: south of the equator, shadows point south at noon

snav-03-c1.text: Society for Popular Astronomy. Getting your bearings. Young Stargazers (Society for Popular Astronomy).
snav-03-c1.quote: If you could speed up the slow movement of the stars you would see them wheeling anticlockwise around this point.
snav-03-c1.claim: the whole sky seems to wheel anticlockwise around a point in the northern sky

snav-03-c1.text: Society for Popular Astronomy. Getting your bearings. Young Stargazers (Society for Popular Astronomy).
snav-03-c1.quote: It just happens that there is a fairly bright star close to the sky’s north pole.
snav-03-c1.claim: a fairly bright star sits close to that point

snav-03-c1.text: Royal Museums Greenwich. Ursa Minor (Little Bear) and Polaris. Royal Observatory Greenwich.
snav-03-c1.quote: The reason Polaris is so important is that it is almost directly above the North Pole. This means you can use it like a compass to find north.
snav-03-c1.claim: Because it is almost directly above the North Pole, you can use it like a compass

snav-03-c1.text: Royal Museums Greenwich. Ursa Minor (Little Bear) and Polaris. Royal Observatory Greenwich.
snav-03-c1.quote: the angle of the star above the horizon gives you your latitude
snav-03-c1.claim: its angle above the horizon gives you your latitude

snav-03-c1.text: Joseph Genz, Jerome Aucan, Mark Merrifield, Ben Finney, Korent Joel, Alson Kelen (2009). Wave navigation in the Marshall Islands: comparing indigenous and Western scientific knowledge of the ocean. Oceanography.
snav-03-c1.claim: Seafarers settled the islands of Remote Oceania 3,500 to 4,000 years ago

snav-03-c1.text: Joseph Genz, Jerome Aucan, Mark Merrifield, Ben Finney, Korent Joel, Alson Kelen (2009). Wave navigation in the Marshall Islands: comparing indigenous and Western scientific knowledge of the ocean. Oceanography.
snav-03-c1.quote: They developed navigational techniques to sail their deep-sea voyaging canoes over hundreds, and in some cases thousands, of kilometers of ocean without the aid of instruments or charts.
snav-03-c1.claim: sailing hundreds and sometimes thousands of kilometres without instruments or charts

snav-03-c1.text: Nainoa Thompson. Finding a Way: 1974-1980. Polynesian Voyaging Society archive.
Nainoa Thompson. Finding a Way: 1974-1980. Polynesian Voyaging Society archive.
snav-03-c1.quote: Kawika Kapahulehua skippered the canoe, and Mau Piailug was the navigator.
snav-03-c1.claim: sailed from Hawaiʻi to Tahiti with Mau Piailug

snav-03-c1.claim: with Mau Piailug, from the island of Satawal in Micronesia, as navigator

snav-03-c1.text: Nainoa Thompson. Finding a Way: 1974-1980. Polynesian Voyaging Society archive.
snav-03-c1.quote: Nevertheless, sensing his way over 2,500 miles, using clues from the ocean world and the heavens

snav-03-c1.text: Nainoa Thompson. Finding a Way: 1974-1980. Polynesian Voyaging Society archive.
snav-03-c1.quote: never before had he been south of the equator where he could not see the North Star, a key guide for his travels
snav-03-c1.claim: He had never been south of the equator, where he could not see the North Star.

snav-03-c1.text: Polynesian Voyaging Society. Hawaiian Star Compass. Polynesian Voyaging Society archive.
snav-03-c1.quote: Developed by Nainoa Thompson, Based on the Micronesian Star Compass of Mau Piailug
snav-03-c1.claim: built the Hawaiian star compass on Mau's Micronesian one

snav-03-c1.text: Polynesian Voyaging Society. Hawaiian Star Compass. Polynesian Voyaging Society archive.

snav-03-c2.quote: imagine a distance four-and-one-half to five times the distance between these stars and the horizon

snav-03-c2.claim: Two pointer stars beside it help you tell the true Cross from the False Cross

snav-03-c2.text: Headquarters, Department of the Army (2002). FM 3-05.70: Survival. LSU Law Center (copy of the US Army field manual).

snav-03-c2.claim: the dark patch between them is the Coal Sack

snav-03-c2.text: Headquarters, Department of the Army (2002). FM 3-05.70: Survival. LSU Law Center (copy of the US Army field manual).
snav-03-c2.quote: the North Star can always be found at the same approximate vertical angle above the horizon as the northern line of latitude you are located on

snav-03-c3.text: Society for Popular Astronomy. Getting your bearings. Young Stargazers (Society for Popular Astronomy).
snav-03-c3.quote: a lot of people expect it to be very bright, but it is fairly ordinary
snav-03-c3.claim: People expect it to be very bright, but it is fairly ordinary

snav-03-c3.text: Royal Museums Greenwich. Ursa Minor (Little Bear) and Polaris. Royal Observatory Greenwich.
snav-03-c3.quote: Polaris is interesting to astronomers because it is a pulsating ‘supergiant’
snav-03-c3.claim: Polaris is actually a pulsating supergiant

snav-03-c3.text: Royal Museums Greenwich. Ursa Minor (Little Bear) and Polaris. Royal Observatory Greenwich.
snav-03-c3.quote: However, Polaris does not look very bright to us because it is so far away. Polaris is 431 light years away from Earth
snav-03-c3.claim: at 431 light years away it does not look very bright

snav-03-c3.text: Royal Museums Greenwich. Ursa Minor (Little Bear) and Polaris. Royal Observatory Greenwich.
snav-03-c3.quote: The ancient Greeks realised that Polaris did not mark the pole exactly.
snav-03-c3.claim: The ancient Greeks already knew that Polaris did not mark the pole exactly.

snav-03-c3.text: Royal Museums Greenwich. Ursa Minor (Little Bear) and Polaris. Royal Observatory Greenwich.
snav-03-c3.quote: About 5,000 years ago, a star called Thuban was the Pole Star and in about 5,000 years’ time, a star called Alderamin in the constellation Cepheus will be nearest the pole.
snav-03-c3.claim: about 5,000 years ago it was Thuban, and in about 5,000 years it will be Alderamin, in Cepheus

snav-03-c3.text: Joseph Genz, Jerome Aucan, Mark Merrifield, Ben Finney, Korent Joel, Alson Kelen (2009). Wave navigation in the Marshall Islands: comparing indigenous and Western scientific knowledge of the ocean. Oceanography.
snav-03-c3.quote: Scholars initially interpreted these models as “stick charts,” believing they showed the positions of islands, sailing courses, and sea conditions (Gulick, 1862; Meinicke, 1863).
snav-03-c3.claim: Nineteenth-century scholars read the lattices of sticks as charts of islands and sailing courses.

snav-03-c3.text: Joseph Genz, Jerome Aucan, Mark Merrifield, Ben Finney, Korent Joel, Alson Kelen (2009). Wave navigation in the Marshall Islands: comparing indigenous and Western scientific knowledge of the ocean. Oceanography.
snav-03-c3.quote: Later studies, however, showed that they were not nautical charts or instruments, but rather teaching devices that depicted the direction of predominant swells
snav-03-c3.claim: Later studies showed they were teaching devices showing how the main swells run, bend and cross.

snav-03-c3.text: Joseph Genz, Jerome Aucan, Mark Merrifield, Ben Finney, Korent Joel, Alson Kelen (2009). Wave navigation in the Marshall Islands: comparing indigenous and Western scientific knowledge of the ocean. Oceanography.
snav-03-c3.quote: The navigators detect swells by feeling the motion of the canoe.
snav-03-c3.claim: Marshallese navigators detect the swells by feeling the motion of the canoe

snav-03-c3.text: Joseph Genz, Jerome Aucan, Mark Merrifield, Ben Finney, Korent Joel, Alson Kelen (2009). Wave navigation in the Marshall Islands: comparing indigenous and Western scientific knowledge of the ocean. Oceanography.
snav-03-c3.quote: Captain Korent Joel, one of the last traditional navigators in the Marshall Islands
snav-03-c3.claim: one of the last traditional navigators in the Marshall Islands

snav-03-c3.text: Joseph Genz, Jerome Aucan, Mark Merrifield, Ben Finney, Korent Joel, Alson Kelen (2009). Wave navigation in the Marshall Islands: comparing indigenous and Western scientific knowledge of the ocean. Oceanography.
snav-03-c3.quote: Captain Korent guided a yacht 220 km between two atolls using traditional navigation techniques.
snav-03-c3.claim: guided a yacht 220 km between two atolls by the old methods

snav-03-c3.text: Joseph Genz, Jerome Aucan, Mark Merrifield, Ben Finney, Korent Joel, Alson Kelen (2009). Wave navigation in the Marshall Islands: comparing indigenous and Western scientific knowledge of the ocean. Oceanography.
snav-03-c3.quote: Navigators identified a superposition of incident swells with reflected waves 40 km upstream of islands. These reflected waves were too weak to be detected by the wave buoy
snav-03-c3.claim: Navigators described waves reflected off islands 40 km away, too weak for the scientists

snav-03-c3.text: Polynesian Voyaging Society. Hawaiian Star Compass. Polynesian Voyaging Society archive.
snav-03-c3.quote: it flies out to sea in the morning to fish (range about 40 miles) and returns to land at night to rest
snav-03-c3.claim: the noio, a tern, flies out to sea in the morning to fish, ranging about 40 miles, and returns to land at night

snav-03-c3.text: Nainoa Thompson. Finding a Way: 1974-1980. Polynesian Voyaging Society archive.
snav-03-c3.quote: The 'iwa bird is pelagic and we see it all the way across the ocean.
snav-03-c3.claim: Ocean-going birds such as the ʻiwa are no use

snav-03-c3.text: Nainoa Thompson. Finding a Way: 1974-1980. Polynesian Voyaging Society archive.
snav-03-c3.quote: Following these birds will not help you find land.
snav-03-c3.claim: following them will not help you find land

snav-04-c1.text: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information. Wandering of the Geomagnetic Poles. NOAA NCEI.
snav-04-c1.quote: The WMM representation of the field includes a magnetic dipole at the center of Earth.
snav-04-c1.claim: Its field behaves roughly like a giant bar magnet at the centre of the planet

snav-04-c1.text: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information. Wandering of the Geomagnetic Poles. NOAA NCEI.
snav-04-c1.quote: The axis of the dipole is currently inclined at 9.21° to Earth's rotation axis.
snav-04-c1.claim: tilted about 9 degrees from the axis the Earth spins on

snav-04-c1.text: Royal Museums Greenwich (2019). True north and magnetic north: what's the difference?. Royal Museums Greenwich.
snav-04-c1.quote: Magnetic north is the direction that a compass needle points to as it aligns with the Earth’s magnetic field.
snav-04-c1.claim: A compass needle simply lines up with the local field

snav-04-c1.text: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information. Wandering of the Geomagnetic Poles. NOAA NCEI.
snav-04-c1.quote: In 1831, James Clark Ross located the north dip pole position in northern Canada.
snav-04-c1.claim: James Clark Ross located the north magnetic pole in northern Canada in 1831

snav-04-c1.text: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information. Wandering of the Geomagnetic Poles. NOAA NCEI.
snav-04-c1.quote: The most recent survey determined that the Pole is moving approximately north-northwest at 55km per year.
snav-04-c1.claim: the most recent survey found it moving north-north-west at about 55 km a year

snav-04-c1.text: Amorina Kingdon (2019). The South Pointing Spoon. Hakai Magazine.
snav-04-c1.quote: This is a replica of the aptly named south pointing spoon, thought to be the first magnetized object ever used to tell direction.
snav-04-c1.claim: The first compass was probably a spoon.

snav-04-c1.text: Amorina Kingdon (2019). The South Pointing Spoon. Hakai Magazine.
snav-04-c1.quote: written during China’s Han dynasty around 60 CE
snav-04-c1.claim: Around 60 CE, during China's Han dynasty

snav-04-c1.text: Amorina Kingdon (2019). The South Pointing Spoon. Hakai Magazine.
snav-04-c1.quote: “When the south pointing spoon is thrown upon the ground,” writes author Wang Chong, “it comes to rest pointing at the south.”
snav-04-c1.claim: the writer Wang Chong described a south-pointing spoon that comes to rest pointing south when thrown on the ground

snav-04-c1.text: Susan Silverman. Compass, China, 220 BCE. Smith College Museum of Ancient Inventions.
snav-04-c1.quote: The spoon-shaped instrument was placed on a cast bronze plate
snav-04-c1.claim: set on a bronze plate marked with directions

snav-04-c1.text: Susan Silverman. Compass, China, 220 BCE. Smith College Museum of Ancient Inventions.
snav-04-c1.quote: Primarily, the compass was used for geomancy for a long time before it was used for navigation
snav-04-c1.claim: For a long time it served geomancy, choosing sites and times for buildings and burials, rather than navigation.

snav-04-c1.text: Amorina Kingdon (2019). The South Pointing Spoon. Hakai Magazine.
snav-04-c1.quote: This replica of the south pointing spoon and its plate was made in the 20th century
snav-04-c1.claim: The spoons you see today are twentieth-century replicas built from those descriptions.

snav-04-c1.text: Amorina Kingdon (2019). The South Pointing Spoon. Hakai Magazine.
snav-04-c1.quote: By the 11th century, people had noticed that needles rubbed with lodestone also aligned north-south and were suspending magnetized needles on silk string or floating them in bowls of water.
snav-04-c1.claim: By the 11th century people had noticed that needles rubbed with lodestone also lined up north-south, and they floated them in bowls of water or hung them on silk.

snav-04-c1.text: Susan Silverman. Compass, China, 220 BCE. Smith College Museum of Ancient Inventions.
snav-04-c1.quote: They also had observed that needles cooled from red heat and held in the north-south orientation (the earth's axis) would become magnetic.
snav-04-c1.claim: Chinese scholars also found that needles cooled from red heat while lying north-south became magnetic.

snav-04-c1.text: Amorina Kingdon (2019). The South Pointing Spoon. Hakai Magazine.
snav-04-c1.quote: “The pilots steer by the stars at night, and in the daytime by the sun; in dark weather, they look at the south pointing needle,” writes historian Zhu Yu in the early 12th century.
snav-04-c1.claim: pilots steer by the stars at night and the sun by day, and in dark weather look at the south-pointing needle

snav-04-c1.text: Royal Museums Greenwich (2019). True north and magnetic north: what's the difference?. Royal Museums Greenwich.
snav-04-c1.quote: What we do know is that here in Europe, they were being used as early as the 12th century, and even earlier in China.
snav-04-c1.claim: Compasses were in use in Europe by the 12th century.

snav-04-c2.text: Glyn Dodwell (2019). A tale of three norths. OS GetOutside (Ordnance Survey).
snav-04-c2.quote: There are in fact three different Norths!
snav-04-c2.claim: Ordnance Survey reminds walkers that there are three norths.

snav-04-c2.text: Glyn Dodwell (2019). A tale of three norths. OS GetOutside (Ordnance Survey).
snav-04-c2.quote: The geographical north where the ‘North Pole’ is, as defined by the rotation of the Earth.
snav-04-c2.claim: True north is the geographic North Pole.

snav-04-c2.text: Glyn Dodwell (2019). A tale of three norths. OS GetOutside (Ordnance Survey).
snav-04-c2.quote: The north to which your compass points.
snav-04-c2.claim: Magnetic north is where your compass points.

snav-04-c2.text: Ordnance Survey. How to use a compass. OS GetOutside (Ordnance Survey).
snav-04-c2.quote: North is 0 or 360 degrees, east is 90 degrees, south is 180 degrees, and west is 270 degrees.
snav-04-c2.claim: measured in degrees from north: east is 90, south 180 and west 270

snav-04-c2.text: Ordnance Survey. How to use a compass. OS GetOutside (Ordnance Survey).
snav-04-c2.quote: Line up point A and B with either the side of your compass or one of the black lines running down the base plate
snav-04-c2.claim: Lay the compass on the map with its long edge joining where you are to where you want to go

snav-04-c2.text: Ordnance Survey. How to use a compass. OS GetOutside (Ordnance Survey).
snav-04-c2.quote: Line up the orienting lines with the map’s north-south grid lines
snav-04-c2.claim: Turn the dial until the orienting lines run parallel to the map

snav-04-c2.text: Glyn Dodwell (2019). A tale of three norths. OS GetOutside (Ordnance Survey).
snav-04-c2.quote: The angle between Magnetic North and Grid North is the Grid Magnetic Angle (GMA) and it is this angle that needs to be applied when converting between Magnetic and Grid bearings.
snav-04-c2.claim: Apply the grid magnetic angle printed on your map.

snav-04-c2.text: Ordnance Survey. How to use a compass. OS GetOutside (Ordnance Survey).
snav-04-c2.claim: one OS practice route adds 1 degree

snav-04-c2.text: Ordnance Survey. How to use a compass. OS GetOutside (Ordnance Survey).
snav-04-c2.quote: Turn your whole body until the red needle lines up with the orienting arrow
snav-04-c2.claim: turn your whole body until the red needle lines up with the orienting arrow

snav-04-c2.text: Ordnance Survey. How to use a compass. OS GetOutside (Ordnance Survey).
snav-04-c2.quote: Try to avoid looking at the compass all the time as you walk, as this is less accurate than using a more distant target.
snav-04-c2.claim: rather than staring at the needle as you go

snav-04-c2.text: Ordnance Survey. How to use a compass. OS GetOutside (Ordnance Survey).
snav-04-c2.quote: mobile phones, magnetic buttons, metal belts and similar can ‘deflect’ the compass needle, making it inaccurate
snav-04-c2.claim: Keep the compass away from mobile phones, magnetic buttons, metal belts and the like, which can deflect the needle.

snav-04-c2.text: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information. Geomagnetism Frequently Asked Questions. NOAA NCEI.
snav-04-c2.quote: It is important to understand that local magnetic anomalies exceeding 10 degrees of declination, although rare, do exist.
snav-04-c2.claim: local magnetic anomalies exceeding 10 degrees, although rare, do exist

snav-04-c2.claim: one area of Minnesota has 16 degrees east declination a few miles from 12 degrees west

snav-04-c2.quote: You may want a GPS device, but those sometimes do not receive a signal or the battery fails.

snav-04-c3.text: Royal Museums Greenwich (2019). True north and magnetic north: what's the difference?. Royal Museums Greenwich.

snav-04-c3.claim: Most of the time, compasses do not point precisely towards the North Pole

snav-04-c3.text: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information. Geomagnetism Frequently Asked Questions. NOAA NCEI.

snav-04-c3.claim: The angle between magnetic north and true north is the declination

snav-04-c3.quote: D is considered positive when the angle measured is east of true north and negative when west.
snav-04-c3.claim: counted as east or west of true north

snav-04-c3.claim: at the poles themselves the field points straight down and a compass does not show direction at all

snav-04-c3.quote: the GMA given for each map is correct only at the time of printing
snav-04-c3.claim: correct only at the time of printing

snav-04-c3.text: Royal Museums Greenwich (2019). True north and magnetic north: what's the difference?. Royal Museums Greenwich.

snav-04-c3.claim: In September 2019, compasses at Greenwich pointed to true north for the first time in about 360 years.

snav-04-c3.quote: The line of zero declination, called the agonic, is moving westward at a present rate of around 20 km per year.
snav-04-c3.claim: The line of zero declination is moving west at around 20 km a year

snav-04-c3.text: BGS Press (2019). Hold onto your compass: true north and magnetic north cross at Greenwich for first time in 360 years. British Geological Survey.
snav-04-c3.quote: By 2040, all compasses will probably point eastwards of true north.
snav-04-c3.claim: by 2040 all compasses in the UK will probably point east of true north

snav-04-c3.text: BGS Press (2019). Hold onto your compass: true north and magnetic north cross at Greenwich for first time in 360 years. British Geological Survey.

snav-04-c3.claim: in 1926 the electrification of the railways made measurements there impossible, and the instruments moved to Abinger, south of London

snav-05-c1.text: Headquarters, Department of the Army (2002). FM 3-05.70: Survival. LSU Law Center (copy of the US Army field manual).

snav-05-c1.text: Headquarters, Department of the Army (2002). FM 3-05.70: Survival. LSU Law Center (copy of the US Army field manual).

snav-05-c1.claim: so is the southern side of boulders and large rocks

snav-05-c1.text: Headquarters, Department of the Army (2002). FM 3-05.70: Survival. LSU Law Center (copy of the US Army field manual).

snav-05-c1.claim: a stream, a trail, a road, anything you can naturally follow

snav-05-c1.text: US Forest Service. If You Get Lost. USDA Forest Service.
snav-05-c1.quote: This is often a difficult path but could lead to a trail or road. Again, this could be very dangerous.
snav-05-c1.claim: it could lead to a trail or road, and it could also be very dangerous

snav-05-c1.text: Society for Popular Astronomy. Getting your bearings. Young Stargazers (Society for Popular Astronomy).

snav-05-c1.quote: It is more or less due south at that time
snav-05-c1.claim: at midday the sun is more or less due south

snav-05-c2.text: Headquarters, Department of the Army (2002). FM 3-05.70: Survival. LSU Law Center (copy of the US Army field manual).
snav-05-c2.quote: Remember size, ratio, angularity, straight lines, and square corners are not found in nature.
snav-05-c2.claim: straight lines and square corners are not found in nature

snav-05-c2.text: Mountain Rescue England and Wales. Safety. Mountain Rescue England and Wales.
snav-05-c2.quote: Six good long blasts in a minute. Stop for one minute. Repeat.
snav-05-c2.claim: six good long blasts in a minute

snav-05-c2.text: Mountain Rescue England and Wales. Safety. Mountain Rescue England and Wales.
snav-05-c2.quote: Continue until someone reaches you and don’t stop because you hear a reply. Your whistle blasts may be a direction finder.
snav-05-c2.claim: not to stop just because you hear a reply, since your blasts may be guiding the team in

snav-05-c2.text: Headquarters, Department of the Army (2002). FM 3-05.70: Survival. LSU Law Center (copy of the US Army field manual).
snav-05-c2.quote: In some documented cases, they have been heard up to 1.6 kilometers (3/4 mile) away.
snav-05-c2.claim: Whistles have been heard up to 1.6 km away.

snav-05-c2.text: Headquarters, Department of the Army (2002). FM 3-05.70: Survival. LSU Law Center (copy of the US Army field manual).
snav-05-c2.quote: On a sunny day, a mirror is your best signaling device.
snav-05-c2.claim: On a sunny day a mirror is your best signalling device

snav-05-c2.text: Headquarters, Department of the Army (2002). FM 3-05.70: Survival. LSU Law Center (copy of the US Army field manual).

snav-05-c2.claim: Catch the glare on your palm, hold up two fingers in a V with the aircraft between them

snav-05-c2.text: Headquarters, Department of the Army (2002). FM 3-05.70: Survival. LSU Law Center (copy of the US Army field manual).
snav-05-c2.quote: Then move the mirror slowly and rhythmically up and down off your hand and onto the aim point
snav-05-c2.claim: rock the mirror slowly off your hand and onto the target

snav-05-c2.claim: By day, three columns of smoke say the same.
